rationale: Advanced prototyping is a fair question for a design tool like Canva, so the axis applies. The evidence pack covers only developer surfaces: Apps SDK, Connect APIs, MCP server, SCIM, audit logs and exports. Nothing documents animation between states, conditional logic or variables, or scroll effects in prototypes.

Canva's first-party docs describe three write-capable surfaces. The official MCP server supports design generation from text, targeted edits to existing designs through natural-language commands, resizing, and asset uploads. The Connect APIs let integrations create and sync designs and assets, and the Apps SDK can add elements to a user's design and automate design tasks. Missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration that agent-driven create/edit works as documented, and clarity on plan gating (resizing requires Pro or above; private integrations require Enterprise).

Canva's official MCP server is a documented surface that lets AI assistants interact with Canva. It explicitly lists 'Design export' to multiple formats (PDF, PNG, JPG, PPTX, MP4) and resizing for different channels, with a documented `resize-design` tool and rate limits. The Connect APIs add a documented REST/OpenAPI surface for integrating design workflows. missing for 10: no independent or hands-on corroboration of export working via agents, no explicit Connect API export endpoint details or screenshot/thumbnail rendering evidence, and resize is gated to Pro-and-above plans.

Canva ships an official MCP server for AI assistants. Its tools can search and retrieve designs and pages, export them as PNG, JPG or PDF (screenshot-like images), and give access to brand kits and templates. The Connect APIs also sync designs and assets. However, the MCP server is aimed at generating and editing designs, not at handing structured design context to a coding agent. Missing for 10: structured frame/layer data, design variables or tokens, component-to-code mappings, any documented design-to-code workflow, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

A live probe confirms a root llms.txt at canva.dev (HTTP 200) indexing Canva's developer documentation. Section-level llms.txt files exist for SCIM, Admin and audit logs, and docs pages are served as agent-friendly .md (connect.md, apps.md, apps/mcp.md), so an agent can be pointed straight at machine-readable docs. Missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration of agents actually consuming these docs; the probed /docs/.md path returned 404, which leaves the scope of markdown coverage less certain.

The evidence shows an in-product Canva AI that can pull in content via pasted links from other platforms for design context, and data imported from third-party sources can feed design generation. That is AI acting on user data inside the product, but it produces designs rather than analysis. Nothing documents AI-generated insights, analysis, or recommendations drawn from the user's data. Missing for 10: any documented AI insight or analysis feature over user data, in-product suggestions or recommendations derived from data, depth of documentation on how Canva AI uses imported data, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

Canva's docs describe programmatic automation building blocks: Connect API integrations that create and sync assets and designs, autofill of Brand Templates from data sources, automatic resizing, and bulk generation. However, any background automation must be built by the user or a developer on these APIs, or driven by an external AI assistant through the MCP server. Nothing in the pack shows a native way to configure automations that run on their own. Missing for 10: native user-configurable automations, scheduling or trigger/webhook mechanisms for unattended background runs, and independent or hands-on evidence of autonomous workflows.

The only evidence of an in-product assistant is a single mention of "Canva AI", where users paste links from other platforms to design with more context. That implies a built-in AI design assistant but says nothing about what tasks it can take on. The MCP server material (natural-language design generation and editing) is about external AI assistants connecting to Canva, so it is not a built-in assistant and is not credited here. Missing for 10: documentation of the built-in Canva AI's capabilities, evidence of multi-step task delegation inside the editor, and any hands-on or independent corroboration.

Canva has no headless mode for the product itself. Its Connect APIs (REST with an OpenAPI description for generating client SDKs) and the MCP server let you drive designs, autofill Brand Templates, bulk-create, resize and export programmatically, which covers API-driven automation. The official CLI is only for building Canva apps, not running Canva in CI, and private integrations are gated to Enterprise plans, with some MCP tools limited to Pro and above. Missing for 10: documented CI/pipeline usage, non-interactive service-account auth for unattended runs, independent hands-on corroboration of headless automation, and ungated availability across plans.

Canva has its own AI (Canva AI), so acting as an MCP client is a fair question for this product. The evidence, however, only documents Canva publishing its own MCP server for external AI assistants to call (the server role). Nothing shows Canva or Canva AI connecting to third-party MCP servers or using their tools.

Canva documents an official MCP server that lets AI assistants work with its design capabilities (generation, editing, discovery, asset and brand management, export, comments), and the probe confirms the docs page exists; there is also a user-facing AI Connector path for personal assistants. Some tools, such as resizing, are limited to Canva Pro and above. Missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration of connecting an agent, and concrete setup/authentication details (endpoint, client configuration) in the evidence.

Canva's first-party docs describe an official MCP server and AI Connector that let users operate Canva through natural language from their own AI assistants. Documented capabilities include text-to-design generation, targeted design edits via natural-language commands, search and discovery, export and resize, asset and brand management, and comments. A probe also confirms the MCP docs exist. missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration that natural-language operation works as claimed, and detail on Canva's native in-editor AI commands (only a thin Canva AI mention); some tools are also gated to Pro and above.

Canva documents an official command-line tool, but it is scoped to creating and managing Canva Apps SDK apps (canva-docs-14, canva-probe-5), not to driving core Canva work like designs, exports, or assets from the terminal. The evidence describes it only in a single line, with no detail on commands, authentication, or scripted or agent use. Missing for 10: a CLI covering core Canva operations, documented command reference and agent/automation-friendly usage, independent or hands-on corroboration.

Canva documents public Connect APIs for creating and syncing designs, assets, comments, autofill, resize and export, and publishes an OpenAPI description for generating client SDKs. Admin, SCIM and audit-log APIs, an official MCP server and an llms.txt index round out programmatic control. The probe misses on guessed OpenAPI paths only show the spec isn't at a standard well-known location, not that it doesn't exist. Missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration of API usage, an OpenAPI spec at a discoverable standard path, and broad access without plan gating (private integrations require Enterprise; some MCP tools require Pro and above).

Canva offers APIs for agents to use: the Connect APIs, private integrations, and an official MCP server. That makes scoped credentials a fair question, but none of the evidence describes credential issuance, OAuth scopes, permission scoping or least-privilege tokens for agents. Absence of evidence for an applicable capability is "none".

Canva ships an official Apps SDK for building apps inside the editor, with a quickstart and an official CLI for creating and managing apps, plus distribution via the Apps Marketplace or private team sharing. For the Connect APIs, however, Canva provides only an OpenAPI description that developers run through code-generation tools to produce their own client SDKs, rather than first-party language SDKs. Missing for 10: official prebuilt client SDKs for the Connect APIs, documented language coverage, and independent or hands-on corroboration of the SDK developer experience.

Webhooks are a fair axis for a SaaS platform with Connect APIs. The only related evidence is a docs line about receiving and replying to Canva comments from any platform, plus a note that Connect APIs can sync comments; this implies some event delivery but never explicitly names webhooks or event subscriptions. Missing for 10: explicit webhook/event-subscription documentation, list of subscribable event types, signature verification and delivery/retry details, hands-on corroboration.

The evidence only glancingly shows a built-in "Canva AI" that users can feed pasted links to "design with more context" (canva-docs-10). Natural-language design generation and editing are documented, but through the MCP server for external AI assistants rather than inside the editor (canva-docs-33, canva-docs-18). Missing for 10: evidence of in-editor image generation, background removal, content-aware fill, and copy/text suggestions, plus any first-party product docs or hands-on corroboration of the editor's AI features.

Canva publishes developer APIs (Connect, SCIM, Admin) and an OpenAPI description of the Connect APIs for generating client SDKs, so this axis applies. However, nothing in the evidence describes an interactive API explorer, a 'try it' console, or runnable examples. Probes of common OpenAPI paths also returned 404. A spec meant for code generation is not the interactive, runnable reference the story asks for.

Canva's first-party docs say it provides an OpenAPI description of the Connect APIs, intended for generating client SDKs with code-generation libraries (canva-docs-31, canva-docs-36, canva-docs-13). The probe's 404s at guessed root paths (/openapi.json, /swagger.json, etc.) only show the spec isn't at conventional locations; they do not contradict that the spec exists, so this is not a dispute. Missing for 10: a confirmed download URL or hands-on fetch of the spec, independent corroboration, and evidence that equivalent specs exist for the SCIM, Admin and audit-log APIs.

A sandbox or test environment is a fair ask for a SaaS platform with developer APIs (Connect APIs, Apps SDK, MCP server), so the axis applies. Nothing in the evidence pack mentions a sandbox, test tenant, or isolated non-production environment. Team apps, private integrations and the app-creation CLI are distribution and development tooling, not data isolation from production.

Canva clearly ships public APIs (Connect, SCIM, Admin, Apps SDK, MCP server), so API versioning and deprecation policy is a fair question for this product. However, nothing in the evidence pack mentions API versioning, version identifiers, or a documented deprecation or sunset policy. The OpenAPI description and the API listings do not establish either.

Canva's docs mention generating personalized content in bulk from your own data (canva-docs-8), importing third-party data for 'Bulk create' (canva-docs-32), autofilling Brand Templates from data sources (canva-docs-7), and automatically creating resized versions of designs (canva-docs-16). That covers bulk design generation, but the evidence is one-line marketing mentions, and the MCP resize tool is rate-limited to 20 req/min (canva-docs-6), which suggests per-item calls rather than true batch operations. Missing for 10: documented batch API endpoints, bulk edit/move/delete/export across many existing designs or assets, AI/MCP-driven bulk workflows, detailed docs on Bulk create limits, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

Event-driven automation such as rules, triggers, or webhooks is a fair axis for a SaaS design platform like Canva. However, the evidence pack documents no rule engine, no webhook or event subscription mechanism, and no way to define triggers that run actions automatically. The cited capabilities (Connect APIs, Autofill and Bulk create, MCP tools, audit logs) are all on-demand or programmatic calls. A vague mention of receiving comments from other platforms does not show user-defined event-to-action rules.

Scheduling recurring jobs or workflows is a fair question for a design and automation SaaS platform, so the axis applies. The evidence covers on-demand automation only: Connect APIs, autofill of Brand Templates, bulk create, resize and MCP tools. Nothing in the pack mentions scheduling, cron-like triggers or recurring execution.

Canva offers automation surfaces such as Autofill, Bulk create, the Apps SDK, the Connect APIs and the MCP server, so versioning and rolling back automations is a fair question for it. The evidence shows no way to version, review diffs of, or roll back those automations. Audit logs only record user activities like app installs and exports, and the CLI only creates and manages apps; neither describes automation version history or rollback.

Canva's first-party docs describe an Apps SDK for building apps that run inside the Canva editor, adding elements, importing content and automating design tasks. A CLI supports creating and managing these apps, and they can be distributed publicly via the Apps Marketplace or privately to a team, with a monetization path. Missing for 10: no evidence of TypeScript typings or sample/starter code, and no independent or hands-on corroboration of the SDK developer experience.

The developer docs name Canva's plan tiers (Pro, Business, Enterprise) and show some per-feature gating. An MCP/AI-connector tool is marked "Pro and above," and private Connect integrations are limited to Enterprise. This is only a glancing view of tiering inside technical docs, not a published pricing page. Missing for 10: a published pricing page with prices, seat types and per-seat structure, a comprehensive AI-feature gating matrix across plans, and independent corroboration.

Canva's developer docs confirm that designs carry comments. Users can receive and reply to comments (threaded replies), add comments to designs, and sync comments via the Connect APIs. However, the evidence is integration-focused and never mentions @-mentioning teammates or resolving threads. Missing for 10: evidence of @mentions, thread resolution, first-party in-editor commenting docs, independent or hands-on corroboration.

Design-to-code handoff is a fair question for a design tool, so the axis applies. However, the evidence shows no component-to-code mapping and no code output from designs. The documented exports are PDF, PNG, JPG, PPTX and MP4 assets, and the OpenAPI-based SDK generation produces API client libraries rather than code derived from designs.

The only related evidence is that brand kits can be accessed and managed through the MCP server (canva-docs-20), and that Brand Templates help teams produce on-brand designs (canva-docs-15). That loosely suggests centrally managed brand styles, but nothing describes token or variable management. missing for 10: explicit color/spacing/typography tokens or variables, modes/themes (e.g., light/dark) applied across designs, documentation of how brand kit values propagate to designs, independent or hands-on corroboration.

Canva's docs describe design export in multiple formats (PDF, PNG, JPG, PPTX, MP4) through its MCP server and automated resizing to new dimensions and formats. That covers whole-design, multi-format export, but nothing in the evidence shows the per-layer production-asset workflow the story asks for. Missing for 10: SVG export evidence, per-layer/element export presets, export scale multipliers, slices, and any independent or hands-on corroboration.

Free-tier capability is a fair question for a design SaaS like Canva, but the evidence pack is almost entirely developer and API documentation. Nothing in it describes what the free plan includes for editing or collaboration. The only plan-related item says the resize tool is limited to Pro and above, which does not show the free tier supports real design work.

Developer handoff is a fair question for a design tool like Canva. The evidence pack covers the Apps SDK, Connect APIs, MCP server, exports and asset management. Nothing in it describes a layer-inspect mode, measurements, style extraction, or CSS/iOS/Android code snippets, and nothing shows such access is available without an editor seat.

Clickable prototyping is a fair question for a visual design tool like Canva, so the axis applies. However, the evidence pack covers only developer surfaces: the Apps SDK, Connect APIs, the MCP server, SCIM/admin APIs and audit logs. Nothing in it mentions linking screens, interaction triggers, transitions or overlays.

Canva's first-party MCP docs say it supports design generation, creating designs "from text descriptions and specifications," and design editing, applying "targeted modifications to existing designs through natural language commands." Separate docs also reference Canva AI designing with pasted-link context. Together these cover both halves of the story, generating and editing designs from prompts. Missing for 10: the evidence is only one-line feature bullets centred on the MCP/AI-assistant route, with no depth on layout or mockup quality and no independent or hands-on proof that the generated designs are usable.

Nothing in the evidence shows Canva's native design format is open or documented. Portability outside the editor comes only through exports to standard formats (PDF, PNG, JPG, PPTX, MP4) via the MCP server and the Connect APIs, which can create and sync designs. These exports give some toolability but are converted outputs, not the editable native format. Missing for 10: a documented or open native design file format, lossless round-trip import/export of editable designs, and independent corroboration of how well exports preserve design structure.

Canva exposes a broad programmatic surface. The Connect APIs create and sync assets, designs and comments, and support Brand Template autofill, bulk creation, resizing, and send-to-platform. The official MCP server covers design generation, natural-language editing, discovery, export, asset and brand management, and comments. Admin, SCIM and audit-log APIs handle team management. Nothing in the evidence claims or shows UI parity, though: editing is limited to targeted natural-language modifications, the Apps SDK runs inside the editor rather than as a headless API, and some capabilities are plan-gated (resize is Pro and above; private integrations require Enterprise). Missing for 10: an explicit API/UI parity claim, element-level design editing via an external API, ungated access to all features across plans, and hands-on or independent corroboration of coverage.

Canva documents exporting designs in multiple widely used formats (PDF, PNG, JPG, PPTX, MP4) through its MCP server. Its Connect APIs and design discovery tools can retrieve and sync designs and assets, so a scripted per-design export path exists. However, nothing shows a full-account or bulk data export, and the formats listed are rendered outputs rather than an open, editable design source format, so leaving with everything intact is only partly supported. Missing for 10: documented bulk or full-account export, export of editable designs in an open native format, coverage of non-design data (comments, brand kits, folders), independent or hands-on corroboration.

Whether a software product's source is available under an open license is a fair question for any SaaS design tool, so the axis applies. Nothing in the evidence pack says Canva's source is published or openly licensed. The evidence covers APIs, an SDK, a CLI, an MCP server and an OpenAPI description, but none of these is product source code.

Self-hosting is a fair axis for a design SaaS like Canva, but the evidence pack contains nothing showing the core editor can be deployed on your own infrastructure. All cited material describes cloud-hosted integration surfaces: the Apps SDK, Connect APIs, the MCP server, SCIM, Admin API and audit logs.

Canva's Apps SDK brings new design and editing experiences into the editor, including importing content, adding elements and automating tasks. Apps can be published publicly through an Apps Marketplace, with a monetization path and a CLI for building apps, so marketplace-based editor extensibility is clearly documented. missing for 10: evidence of the marketplace's size or community breadth, concrete examples of icon, data-filler or accessibility-checker apps, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

Choosing a data-storage region is a fair question for a cloud SaaS design platform like Canva, so the axis applies. However, nothing in the evidence pack mentions data residency or region selection. The cited docs cover the Apps SDK, Connect APIs, SCIM, audit logs, the Admin API and the MCP server, none of which address where data is stored.

Canva is a SaaS design platform with AI features, so an AI-training opt-out is a fair question. However, nothing in the evidence pack covers data-use or training controls. The pack covers only developer APIs, the MCP server, SCIM, audit logs and app tooling, so there is no evidence that users can stop their data being used to train AI models.

Data retention and deletion controls are a fair privacy question for a SaaS design platform like Canva, so the axis applies. The evidence pack covers the Apps SDK, Connect APIs, the MCP server, SCIM provisioning, the Admin API and audit logs. None of it documents retention policies, data deletion, or controls over how AI features use or keep user data.

Opting out of telemetry and usage tracking is a fair privacy question for a SaaS design platform like Canva, so the axis applies. The evidence pack covers APIs, the MCP server, SCIM, and audit logs, but contains nothing about user-facing telemetry, analytics opt-out, or tracking controls. The audit logs record team activity for admins and are not an opt-out mechanism.

Real-time co-editing is a fair question for a design tool, so the axis applies. However, the evidence pack is developer documentation that only mentions comments, audit logs, and teams editing brand templates. Nothing documents simultaneous editing, live cursors, or instant sync; the 'sync' in the Connect APIs refers to integrations syncing assets, not live multiplayer.

Canva's docs only show automated design resizing, which creates new versions of a design in different dimensions, formats, or aspect ratios. That is adjacent to the story but not the same as frames that reflow responsively. Nothing in the evidence covers auto layout, constraints, or layout grids. Missing for 10: auto layout behavior, resizing constraints, responsive layout grids, frames that flex live like real UIs, and hands-on corroboration.

Reusable linked components with variants are a fair question for a design tool like Canva, so the axis applies. The evidence covers only Brand Templates, autofill and bulk creation. Templates spawn independent copies, and nothing in the pack shows components with variants, per-instance overrides, or a live link back to a source component.

Self-hosting under an open-source license is a fair question for a design platform, since open-source self-hostable design tools exist, so the axis applies. The evidence pack only documents cloud-hosted integration surfaces: the Apps SDK, Connect APIs, MCP server, SCIM and audit logs. Nothing shows a self-hostable or open-source distribution of the platform.

The evidence shows only adjacent capabilities. Brand Templates can be made accessible to teams for on-brand design (canva-docs-15), and brand kits and templates can be accessed and managed (canva-docs-20), which partly covers sharing styles and templates across a team. Nothing describes publishing reusable components into a shared library that links into other files, or propagating updates when the source changes. Missing for 10: a shared component library linked across files and projects, a controlled update or versioning flow when the source changes, and hands-on or independent corroboration.

Canva is a design product, so professional vector tooling is a fair question to ask of it. However, the evidence pack covers only developer APIs, the MCP server, brand templates, resizing and natural-language design editing. It never mentions pen/path editing, boolean operations or precise alignment tools.

Version history is a fair axis for a design tool like Canva, but the evidence pack contains nothing about version history, named milestones, comparing versions, or restoring earlier states. The audit logs it mentions record team activity such as exports and settings changes, which is not file-level versioning.

Claude Design says it turns static mockups into shareable interactive prototypes, and its output is real HTML/CSS/JS, which can in principle carry rich behavior. Community users report building animated SVGs, though one notes that SVG export strips animations unless worked around. Nothing documents state-to-state transitions, conditional logic or variables, or scroll effects as prototyping features. Missing for 10: documented animation between prototype states, conditions/variables support, scroll effects, and hands-on corroboration of advanced prototype interactions beyond SVG animation.

Claude Design can be driven from agent contexts: you can work in Claude Code with /design and pull design systems in via /design-sync, and it can be invoked from inside any Claude conversation. So an agent can create and modify designs, but only through Anthropic's own Claude surfaces, not an open programmatic interface. There is no documented write-capable public API (the OpenAPI probes all returned 404) and no first-party MCP server; the PenPot flow is Claude Design writing out through PenPot's MCP, not an MCP for Claude Design itself. Missing for 10: a public write-capable API or MCP server for third-party agents, documentation of the /design command's capabilities, and independent hands-on corroboration of agent-driven design edits.

Claude Design exports to PPTX, PDF, and HTML (docs-8), and agents can reach it conversationally: through /design in Claude Code (docs-6), from inside any Claude conversation (docs-15), or with prompts like "export it as a PDF" (docs-16). A handoff bundle can also be passed to Claude Code (docs-7). However, there is no documented API or OpenAPI spec (probe-3 returned 404 on every path), and a hands-on report says SVG export strips animations unless you work around it (comm-18). Missing for 10: a documented programmatic export/render API or CLI, screenshot/image rendering endpoints, explicit docs for agent-invoked export, and independent corroboration of agent-driven export.

Claude Design hands design context to a coding agent, but only through first-party Claude Code paths: a handoff bundle passed with a single instruction, plus /design and /design-sync commands. A community user calls the handoff skill solid. There is no evidence of a general MCP server or public API that any coding agent could query, and probes found no OpenAPI spec. Missing for 10: an official MCP server or API usable by any agent, documented access to frames, variables, screenshots and component mappings, and agent-agnostic (not Claude Code-only) integration.

Probes confirm a live llms.txt at support.claude.com and a Markdown rendering of the 'Get started with Claude Design' help article, so an agent can be pointed at machine-readable, agent-friendly docs that cover the product. The llms.txt covers the whole Claude Help Center rather than Claude Design specifically, and nothing shows how deep the Design-specific coverage goes. Missing for 10: a Claude Design–specific llms.txt or llms-full.txt, first-party documentation promoting agent-oriented docs, and independent or hands-on confirmation of agents consuming them.

Claude Design is an AI-native tool that imports user data (XLSX, DOCX, PPTX, codebases) and can pull data from connected apps like Salesforce and QuickBooks. Its marketing page shows an example of digging into QuickBooks numbers to plan a promotion. But its documented output is design artifacts and multiple design directions, not analytical insights drawn from the user's data. Missing for 10: documented data-analysis or insight-generation features, evidence that suggestions are grounded in user data rather than design prompts, and independent hands-on corroboration of data-driven insights.

Background automations are a fair question for an AI-native design tool, so the axis applies. However, the evidence only describes interactive, prompt-driven work: generating designs, refining them in conversation, handing off to Claude Code, and pulling data from connected apps on request. Applying the design system "automatically" is a generation default, not a user-configured automation, and nothing shows scheduled, triggered, or unattended background runs.

Claude is the core of the product. Users describe a visual and Claude builds a first version, refines it through conversation, applies the design system automatically, creates custom sliders and packages handoff bundles for Claude Code. Teams can also chat with Claude together. Hands-on reports confirm real delegation, such as a shippable landing page built in hours and a solid handoff skill, though users note the last 20% still needs human judgment and careful prompting. Missing for 10: in-depth first-party docs on the limits of multi-step delegation, and evidence that the assistant reliably self-corrects without repeated user guidance.

Claude Design is presented as an interactive, browser-based design tool driven by conversation, inline comments, direct edits and sliders. Nothing in the pack documents a headless mode, CLI, public API, or CI integration, and the OpenAPI probe returned 404 on every candidate path. The /design and /design-sync commands in Claude Code are interactive slash commands, so they do not show unattended or CI execution.

One community user reports a Claude Design flow into PenPot "via its MCP" that built PenPot components and design tokens, which suggests Claude Design can act as an MCP client. The product page also shows prompts that pull data from Salesforce, QuickBooks, Canva and HubSpot, implying integrations. However, no first-party doc says Claude Design supports adding arbitrary MCP servers, and the PenPot report is unclear about which side hosted the MCP. Missing for 10: first-party documentation of MCP server/connector configuration in Claude Design, clarity on whether custom or remote MCP servers can be added, details on tool-use permissions, and independent hands-on corroboration.

Claude Design is a SaaS design product, so publishing an official MCP server for external agents is a fair question. Nothing in the evidence documents such a server. The PenPot flow (comm-7) uses PenPot's MCP server, which is client-side use and not a Claude Design server. The Claude Code /design-sync and /design integrations are first-party commands, and nothing shows them exposed as an MCP server.

Hands-on users confirm building pages and assets by prompting (comm-6, comm-7, comm-17), though some report it needs repeated nudging (comm-4). Missing for 10: in-depth first-party documentation of the command surface and its limits beyond marketing-level claims.

Claude Design has no dedicated CLI of its own. That gives terminal-based access only through another first-party agent's slash commands.
